answer: Strengths to preserve: concrete, quantified problem evidence (17/19 on paper, 11/19 unsure on repeat doses), candid acknowledgment of unproven assumptions, a clear wedge strategy, and a funding ask tied to specific tests. Recommended improvements, in priority order: (1) Resolve internal inconsistencies. The summary says 25 discovery interviews while the problem section cites 19 crew plus 6 directors (consistent only if explained); state this once clearly. The market math also needs showing: 10,000 ambulances x ~$350 is $3.5M, but the flat $750 tier for 3+ ambulances is not reflected, and the 'conservative' 4,000-agency figure is unsourced. Cite sources (NEMSIS, NHTSA, state registries) and show the calculation. (2) Substantiate the financials. Year-one revenue of $12,000 from 40 ambulances at $350 equals $14,000, and the mix of agencies and tiers is not explained. Provide a bottom-up build (agencies per association channel, conversion rates, sales cycle length, grant timing), a monthly burn and runway view, and a sensitivity case where adoption is half of plan. The year-three break-even at 200 ambulances also needs an explicit cost trajectory, since contractor development is currently funded by savings. (3) Add stronger demand evidence. Verbal willingness to pay from two pilot directors is weak. Convert pilots into signed letters of intent, document what price was discussed, and report pilot depth (112 calls over what period, how many crews, repeat use rates, drop-off, what crews disliked). The 4.4/5 usefulness rating should state sample size and method. Reframe the $7,000 paid-pilot line as the key validation experiment, with pre-defined success criteria (e.g., X of 6 agencies convert at $350 or secure grant funding). (4) Address regulatory, clinical and liability risk head-on. The app records medication doses and timers in a clinical context. Clarify FDA medical device and clinical decision support positioning, HIPAA and business associate obligations for the secure link and dashboard, state EMS data-reporting formats (NEMSIS compliance, which directly affects the stated grant and reporting value proposition), and liability if a timer fails or is misread. Naming a compliance advisor candidate, or a concrete plan and timeline, would be stronger than 'we intend to address.' (5) Sharpen competition analysis. Name specific competitors and compare price, offline capability and deployment time in a table. Several existing ePCR vendors offer offline modes, so the claim that incumbents show little interest in small agencies needs evidence from interviews or pricing research. Explain defensibility beyond first-mover: association endorsements, protocol libraries, data lock-in, switching costs. (6) Make the go-to-market specific. Identify which state associations, whether any have been contacted, their endorsement process, and typical grant cycles and award sizes. Model customer acquisition cost including travel and training time, and reconcile the 90-minute onboarding promise with support costs: $45 per ambulance per year looks optimistic once configuration, training and device support are included. (7) Clarify team commitment and capacity. All four members are students; state time commitments, post-graduation plans, equity split, and how development continues with a part-time contractor. Name the retired EMS director advisor and any clinical or compliance advisors. (8) Tighten structure and framing. Lead with a one-paragraph summary including the ask, traction and the key risk. Add a short risks-and-mitigations section (adoption speed, funding dependence on grants, hardware logistics, data privacy). Replace the slightly hedged market narrative with a defined expansion sequence and the evidence needed to trigger each step. Overall: the idea and discovery work are solid and the tone is credible; the submission would be materially stronger with sourced market sizing, a transparent bottom-up financial model, signed pilot commitments, and a concrete regulatory and compliance plan.
